title: Variables and Sensors
description: A sensor reading is only useful for an instant unless you catch it in a variable. This is where robot.distance() actually earns its keep.

content.value: Call robot.distance() on its own and the number vanishes the instant it's returned — nothing kept it. Store it in a variable, and now you can compare it, print it, or reuse it more than once without asking the sensor again.

This matters more than it looks: calling robot.distance() a second time might return a completely different number, since the robot may have moved between calls. Storing it once in d guarantees your if statement is judging the same reading it just took.

content.title: 🐍 Read, store, decide
content.hint: Store robot.distance() in a variable called d, then write an if/else using it. Try robot.say(d) to see the actual number.

content.value: robot.line() returns two values at once — a pair. Python lets you unpack a pair straight into two variables in one line: left_on, right_on = robot.line().

Key takeaway: a sensor reading only lasts an instant unless a variable captures it. Storing a reading before deciding also guarantees your decision is judging one consistent moment, not two different ones.

quiz.question: Why store robot.distance() in a variable instead of calling it twice — once in a print, once in an if?
options: Both calls always return the exact same number, so it doesn't matter
The robot may have moved between the two calls, so the readings could genuinely differ
robot.distance() can only be called once per program
quiz.explain: Sensor readings reflect the current instant — calling twice risks judging two different moments as if they were one.

quiz.question: What does `left_on, right_on = robot.line()` do?
options: It unpacks the pair robot.line() returns into two separate variables in one line
quiz.explain: Python lets a function that returns a pair be unpacked directly into two named variables at once.
